Iago. The master manipulator of Othello. A military ensign who destroys a general and his beloved wife through calculated lies rooted in racial hatred and professional jealousy. Though often called honest Iago by those he betrays, he is the play's poisoner. He works to transform Othello's love into murderous rage by falsely insinuating that Desdemona has been unfaithful. His racism is personal and systemic. He views Othello as an outsider who has stolen advancement rightfully his, and he weaponizes the prejudices of Venice to accomplish his ruin.

Iago is passed over for promotion to lieutenant in favor of Cassio, a lesser soldier. His resentment festers throughout the play. He frames his malice in racial terms, calling Othello "the Moor" and "an old black ram." Yet his primary wound is professional wounded pride. He is explicitly bisexual in his vengeance. He suspects both Othello and Cassio of sleeping with his wife Emilia, and he uses these jealousies as fuel.

Iago engineers Cassio's drunken brawl and uses it to have him cashiered—fired. Then he works to restore him to favor, positioning himself as Cassio's advocate. He plants innuendo, remarking on Desdemona's unusual closeness to Cassio, dropping hints about infidelity. The coup comes when he steals Desdemona's handkerchief, her first gift from Othello, and plants it in Cassio's room. The handkerchief becomes Othello's "ocular proof." Iago never shows him Cassio and Desdemona together, only circumstantial evidence that Iago himself corrupts.

Iago's power is that he says nothing directly. He feigns honesty, then drops questions: "Did Michael Cassio, when you wooed my lady, know of your love?" This rhetorical innocence is lethal. Othello murders Desdemona in a jealous rage, smothering her on their wedding night. He then murders himself upon learning the truth. Iago is revealed, arrested, and either executed or dies under torture. The play's ending is ambiguous about his final fate.

Iago is believed to derive from Cinthio's Hecatommithi, a work from fifteen sixty-five, where the ensign is unnamed. Shakespeare names him, giving him humanity that makes his evil more complex. His soliloquies are among Shakespeare's most chilling. He explicitly plots and philosophizes his hatred even when alone.

Iago represents the toxic intersection of systemic racism and personal resentment. He is not an otherworldly demon but a plausibly motivated soldier whose prejudices and professional frustrations corrupt him into genocide—one family's annihilation.
